summary_html: Two polygons that have the same number of sides are called similar when two conditions are satisfied. First, each pair of corresponding angles must be equal; this guarantees that the overall shape is the same, even if the size differs. Second, the lengths of corresponding sides must all be in one common ratio, called the scale factor. For example, if a small photograph of a monument is enlarged from 35 mm to 45 mm, every line in the larger picture is 45/35 times the length of the matching line in the smaller picture, while the angles remain unchanged. The scale factor can be written as a fraction or a decimal, and it works both ways: the larger figure can be reduced by the reciprocal ratio to obtain the smaller one. The concept of similarity is useful because it lets us transfer measurements from a model to a real object. If the height of a model tree is 2 cm and the scale factor to the actual tree is 1:50, the real tree is 100 cm tall. In geometry, similarity is denoted by the tilde symbol, for instance ΔABC ~ ΔDEF, meaning that vertex A corresponds to D, B to E, and C to F. The order of the letters is crucial; writing ΔABC ~ ΔEDF would imply a different correspondence and is therefore incorrect. A common misconception is to think that equal perimeters imply similarity; however, two figures can have the same perimeter but different shapes, so the angle condition must also be satisfied. By checking only one pair of corresponding sides and one pair of angles, we cannot guarantee similarity; both the angle equality and the uniform side ratio are required for a valid conclusion.
